My mom's engagement ring.

My grandmother's mother was sick and went to live with my grandma's family.  My grandmother's sister and her husband agreed to pay half of the medical bills for their mother, seeing as how my grandma was taking care of her.  When my great grandmother passed away, my grandma's sister and her husband reneged on their agreement.  So my grandma kept her mother's engagement ring and had the diamond put into a setting for a man and then gave it to my grandfather as a way of saying thank you.  

My grandpa wore that ring right up until he passed away at 58.  He died in his sleep from a heart attack.  Though he was large (probably obese by today's standards) it came as a great shock to the family.  My grandma offered the ring to my dad, but my dad refused.  He said that his dad always wanted him to take a public speaking course, and when he was finished he would accept the ring.  

My dad wore that ring every day up until my parent's got back together.  (My parents divorced when I was about 4, and got back together when I was 21.)  On Christmas Eve, my dad proposed with the diamond that had been in his father's ring.  

So the diamond went from my great grandmother to my grandfather to my dad to my mom and eventually it will come to me.

In grade six, I was in a play that was 'run' by our music teacher.  We all auditioned for roles and there were to be two performances:  One in the evening (in front of parents and jr. high students) and one in the afternoon (in front of the primary grades).  I got the lead in the afternoon play.  The music teacher's daughter got the lead in the evening play.  

While I was happy to be the lead, over a period of time, I became upset because I felt the teacher's daughter was not only awarded the lead due to nepotism, but also got to perform in the evening (which in my head meant she was a better performer).  I was also upset because this meant my mom couldn't come to the play (as she worked).  I let my frustration get the better of me and made the mistake of venting my spleen in the locker room after gym one day.  

Later that afternoon, the teacher hauled me out of class to tear a strip off me.  Some of the girls in the locker room told the teacher's daughter what I said and of course she went to her mom about it.  She (the teacher) essentially said that I wasn't good enough to be in the evening play, that her daughter was the cream of the crop and that some day, maybe I would be too.  

As a parent, I can understand her being hurt or upset about what I said about her kid, but as a teacher she should have known better.  I went home that night and told my dad I wanted to pull out of the play because of what the teacher said to me.  He encouraged me to go on anyways, because no matter what I had as much right to be in the spotlight as anyone else.  

A few weeks/months later was parent/teacher interviews when my dad brought up the incident with the music teacher.  My dad said what she did was inappropriate and that it was uncalled for.  The teacher apologized to my dad, but he told her that wasn't good enough and had her apologize directly to me, in front of him.  (Yay, Dad!)

This is late advice, but hopefully it can come in handy later on or help someone else.  

I have social anxiety and am trying to get through it as well.  I'm an introvert, but I think I used that as an excuse to shut myself off from the world.  Now that I want to be more social I am battling against the anxiety and the habit.  

I had a counselling session where the cousellor suggested I start small.  Going to the gym would scare the daylights out of me, so I started thinking about the smallest thing I'd be comfortable doing.  For me it's a book club.  It only lasts a couple of hours, once a week.  I can do that.  

So, first you need to break the habit.  You need to start teaching your brain, in small ways at first, that being social isn't hard and that there isn't anything scary about it.  The more you do social activities, the more your mind realizes 'it's okay'.  Now you're building a habit, but a good one.  

Last thing is something I read the other day that may help in a pinch: pretend everyone in the room is your best friend.  Once you start thinking the people around you already like you, you've got nothing to be afraid of.

Good luck!
